shilluk_nyakaya.name: send fish and fertility from the river
shilluk_nyakaya.notes: As the crocodile-divinity of the Sobat-White Nile confluence she governs the river's bounty; annual sacrifices at the onset of the rains secure the river's gifts.

sources.reference: W. Hofmayr, Die Schilluk (1925)

shona_dzivaguru.name: command the darkness of night
shona_dzivaguru.notes: In Korekore tradition Dzivaguru is goddess of the earth and of the darkness of night as well as of the waters; she withdrew her light at the close of the primordial age.

sources.reference: G. Fortune & A. Hodza, on Korekore mhondoro tradition; H. Aschwanden, Karanga Mythology

shona_dzivaguru.name: bring the clouds and the rain
shona_dzivaguru.notes: She controls the clouds, rain, pools and streams; the rainmaking priest Karuva at Dande served her before Matope of the Mutapa dynasty defeated him.

sources.reference: D. P. Abraham, 'The Monomotapa Dynasty' (1959); Korekore oral tradition

shipibo_ronin.name: reveal the kené designs to women
shipibo_ronin.notes: Ronin's skin holds every conceivable design; the geometric kené patterns (ronin rao, 'anaconda-medicine') were revealed to Shipibo women through the plant-teachers piripiri and ayahuasca, the vine being the serpent's second self.

sources.reference: B. Illius, ethnography of Shipibo-Conibo kené; A. Gebhart-Sayer, The Cosmos Encoiled

shipibo_yoashiko_inca.name: hoard fire and the cultivated seed
shipibo_yoashiko_inca.notes: The Inca/'culture-donor' Yoashiko (yoashi, 'stingy') withholds fire and cultigens rather than giving them freely; in Shipibo myth-history he is tricked out of these goods so that humankind obtains them.

sources.reference: P. G. Roe, 'The Josho Nahuanbo Are All Wet and Undercooked' (1988); Shipibo myth of the Inca

shona_nehanda.name: promise that her bones will rise again
shona_nehanda.notes: Through her medium Charwe, executed by the British in 1898 for her part in the First Chimurenga, Nehanda is said to have declared that her bones would rise to lead a second, victorious struggle — a prophecy invoked in the liberation war.

sources.reference: D. N. Beach, 'An Innocent Woman, Unjustly Accused?' History in Africa 25 (1998)

slavic_alyosha_popovich.name: defeat his enemies by cunning and trickery
slavic_alyosha_popovich.notes: The youngest of the three principal bogatyrs, characterized in the byliny as a clever priest's son who wins by guile rather than strength.

sources.reference: Russian byliny of the Kiev cycle

slavic_alyosha_popovich.name: slay Tugarin Zmeyevich
slavic_alyosha_popovich.notes: Prays for rain to soak the wings of the dragon-warrior Tugarin so he falls earthbound, then strikes off his head; disguises himself as a deaf pilgrim to approach undetected.

sources.reference: Bylina of Alyosha Popovich and Tugarin
Bylina of Alyosha Popovich and Tugarin
Korekore oral tradition of Dzivaguru, in southern-African folklore collections
Korekore oral tradition of Dzivaguru
A. Gebhart-Sayer, The Cosmos Encoiled (1984)

shabaka.name: Double Crown (pschent) of Upper and Lower Egypt

sources.reference: Royal statuary and reliefs of Shabaka, 25th Dynasty
P. Schebesta, Die Negrito Asiens: Religion und Mythologie (1957); I. H. N. Evans, The Negritos of Malaya (1937)
Rus'-Byzantine treaties (Primary Chronicle, oaths sworn by Perun)
Helmold and Rus' sources; warriors' devotion to Perun
Korekore mythology of Dzivaguru, goddess of earth and night
B. A. Rybakov, Yazychestvo drevnikh slavyan; on Mokosh-Paraskeva-Pyatnitsa
Slovo o polku Igoreve (The Tale of Igor's Campaign)

slavic_lada.gloss: refrain-name invoked in spring and wedding songs; equated with Mars by Długosz

sources.reference: Jan Długosz, Annales seu cronicae incliti regni Poloniae (c. 1455); 15th-c. Polish church prohibitions

slavic_marzanna.gloss: goddess of death and winter; equated with Ceres by Długosz

sources.reference: Jan Długosz, Annales seu cronicae incliti regni Poloniae (c. 1455)
Helmold of Bosau, Chronica Slavorum (c. 1168)
M. L. Daneel, The God of the Matopo Hills (1970)

shona_chaminuka.gloss: the one who is given rain / rainmaker

sources.reference: Shona oral tradition; Encyclopedia of African Religion, 'Chaminuka'

shona_nehanda.gloss: ancestral byname borne by the mhondoro and its mediums

sources.reference: D. N. Beach, History in Africa 25 (1998)
W. Hofmayr, Die Schilluk (1925)

slavic_perun.name: sacrifice and oath at the oak and hilltop sanctuary
slavic_perun.notes: Shrines stood on hilltops or in oak groves; bulls, goats and roosters were offered, and Rus' warriors swore treaties laying down their weapons before Perun (and Veles). A wooden idol with a silver head and golden moustache stood at Vladimir's Kiev sanctuary (980).

sources.reference: Primary Chronicle (Povest' vremennykh let), s.a. 980, 945; Rus'-Byzantine treaty oaths

slavic_mokosh.name: Friday veneration and offerings of yarn and wool
slavic_mokosh.notes: Spinning, weaving and earth-disturbing work were forbidden on Fridays; offerings of wool, yarn and flax were cast into wells and springs. The cult survived under the figure of St Paraskeva-Pyatnitsa.

sources.reference: B. A. Rybakov, Yazychestvo drevnikh slavyan; East Slavic Friday-observance ethnography

slavic_marzanna.name: drowning/burning of the Marzanna effigy
slavic_marzanna.notes: A straw effigy in white cloth, adorned with ribbons, is carried from house to house, then drowned in a river and/or burned to drive out winter, death and disease and usher in spring; the Church attempted to ban the rite in 1420.

sources.reference: Polish, Czech and Slovak folk-custom records (Topienie Marzanny / Vynášení smrti)

slavic_rod.name: bloodless offerings to Rod and the rozhanitsy
slavic_rod.notes: Bread, kasha (groats/kutia), cheese, honey and mead were set out on a 'second table' for Rod and the birth-fairy rozhanitsy at the birth of a child; condemned in medieval Rus' sermons.

sources.reference: 'Word of St Gregory the Theologian on idols' and other 11th-12th c. Old East Slavic sermons against pagan survivals

shona_mwari.name: cave-oracle and rainmaking at the Matonjeni shrines
shona_mwari.notes: At the Matobo (Matopos) shrines, chiefly Njelele, a voice from the cave answers petitioners; custodians clap and sing praises to ask for rain (mukwerera), and offerings of hoes, clay pots of water, tobacco, beads and cloth are left at the shrine.

sources.reference: M. L. Daneel, The God of the Matopo Hills (1970)

shona_chaminuka.name: mhondoro mediumship and rainmaking
shona_chaminuka.notes: Approached only through a chief and the senior spirit-medium (svikiro, famously Pasipamire), Chaminuka descends into his medium to prophesy and make rain; he stands at the apex of the supratribal mhondoro hierarchy.

sources.reference: M. Gelfand, on Shona mhondoro; Encyclopedia of African Religion, 'Chaminuka'

shona_nehanda.name: mhondoro mediumship
shona_nehanda.notes: The Nehanda spirit possesses a chosen female medium (svikiro), through whom she gives oracles, blesses cultivation and the land, and (in 1896-97) sanctioned armed resistance.

sources.reference: D. N. Beach, History in Africa 25 (1998)

serer_roog.name: offerings at the foot of the baobab and at the upright stones
serer_roog.notes: Though transcendent and approached chiefly through the pangool, Roog receives offerings at the foot of sacred trees (the baobab), at the sea and the sacred River Sine, and at the Senegambian standing-stone (upright stone) sanctuaries.

sources.reference: H. Gravrand, La Civilisation Sereer; on aƭat Roog

serer_pangool.name: sacrifice and libation in the sacred forest
serer_pangool.notes: Cattle, poultry, millet, fruit and milk libations are offered to the snake-symbolized pangool at tumuli, sacred groves and standing stones to secure their intercession with Roog and protection of family and land.

sources.reference: H. Gravrand, La Civilisation Sereer; on the pangool cult

senufo_madebele.name: appeasement-offerings to the bush-spirits
senufo_madebele.cadence: before disturbing the bush / as prescribed by diviners
senufo_madebele.notes: Before clearing or cultivating, gifts and sacrifices are made to obtain the madebele's authorization; sandobele diviners prescribe cast-brass charms (yawiige) worn in the spirits' likeness to keep them favorable.

sources.reference: A. Glaze, Art and Death in a Senufo Village (1981)

senufo_maleeo.name: Poro initiation and ancestral funerary rites
senufo_maleeo.notes: As Ancient Mother and tutelary of the Poro society, Katyeleeo is honored in the initiation of young men and in commemorative funerary dances, where the rhythm-pounder figures (deble) are struck on the ground to invoke the primordial ancestors.

sources.reference: A. Glaze, Art and Death in a Senufo Village (1981)

shilluk_nyakaya.name: rainy-season sacrifices to the crocodile-ancestress
shilluk_nyakaya.notes: Special annual sacrifices (a goat being one offering recorded) are made in Nyakaya's honor at the start of the rainy season; she remains revered as a divinity of the Nile and ancestress of the royal house.

sources.reference: W. Hofmayr, Die Schilluk (1925); D. S. Oyler, Shilluk traditions, Sudan Notes and Records

semang_karei.name: blood-throwing offering to avert the thunderstorm
semang_karei.cadence: in emergencies (when a taboo is broken)
semang_karei.notes: When a thunderstorm threatens as punishment for a broken prohibition (terlaid), the offender scrapes blood from the shin and throws it toward the sky and to the earth-deity to appease Karei.

sources.reference: P. Schebesta, Die Negrito Asiens (1957); I. H. N. Evans, The Negritos of Malaya (1937)

attributes.name: thunder-mark (six-spoked rosette)
attributes.notes: A six-rayed wheel/rosette painted on rafters and shields and worn on jewelry as Perun's apotropaic sign.

sources.reference: Slavic folk-art studies of the gromovoi znak (thunder-mark)

attributes.name: miniature iron axe amulet
attributes.notes: Small iron axe-heads worn on necklaces as protective tokens of Perun, recovered archaeologically across the Rus' lands.

sources.reference: Archaeology of Rus' axe-amulets; Slavic religion handbooks
Slavic mythology handbooks on Perun

sacredAnimals.name: bull
sacredAnimals.notes: Bulls (with goats and roosters) were the chief sacrificial victims offered to Perun.

sources.reference: Slavic religion handbooks on Perun's sacrifices

sacredPlants.name: oak
sacredPlants.notes: The oak is Perun's sacred tree; his sanctuaries stood in oak groves, mirroring the Indo-European thunder-deity/oak complex.

sources.reference: Constantine Porphyrogenitus, De administrando imperio (sacred oak of Rus'); Slavic mythology handbooks

sacredPlants.name: iris (perunika)
sacredPlants.notes: The iris is folk-named 'perunika' after the god.

sources.reference: South Slavic folk botany (perunika)

attributes.name: spindle and unspun wool
attributes.notes: Depicted as a tall, large-headed, long-armed woman who spins flax and wool by night, shearing sheep and twining the thread of fate.

sources.reference: B. A. Rybakov, Yazychestvo drevnikh slavyan; East Slavic embroidery iconography

sacredAnimals.name: sheep
sacredAnimals.notes: Patroness of sheep and the shearing of wool.

sources.reference: East Slavic folk tradition of Mokosh/Paraskeva-Pyatnitsa

attributes.name: solar radiance / the sun he carries across the sky
attributes.notes: As son of Svarog the heavenly smith, Dazhbog is the personified sun and giver of daylight, warmth and wealth.

sources.reference: Hypatian Codex interpolation in the Malalas chronicle; Slovo o polku Igoreve

attributes.name: straw effigy in white cloth
attributes.notes: Embodied as a straw figure dressed in white and hung with ribbons and necklaces, carried in procession and drowned/burned.

sources.reference: Polish/Czech/Slovak folk-custom records of Topienie Marzanny

sacredPlants.name: juniper branches
sacredPlants.notes: Green juniper (and evergreen) branches are carried by the procession that bears the effigy from house to house.

sources.reference: Polish folk-custom records of the Marzanna procession

attributes.name: disembodied voice of the cave-oracle
attributes.notes: Mwari manifests not as an image but as a voice issuing from the rock at the Matonjeni/Njelele shrines.

sources.reference: M. L. Daneel, The God of the Matopo Hills (1970)

attributes.name: black ritual cloth
attributes.notes: Black cloth marks the mhondoro medium and the rainmaking spirit's possession-regalia.

sources.reference: Shona mhondoro ethnography

sacredAnimals.name: lion (mhondoro)
sacredAnimals.notes: The royal ancestral spirit is conceived as a 'lion-spirit' (mhondoro means lion), the form the spirit takes when not in its human medium.

sources.reference: M. Gelfand, on the mhondoro lion-spirits of the Shona

sacredAnimals.name: lion (mhondoro)
sacredAnimals.notes: As a royal ancestral mhondoro, the Nehanda spirit is a lion-spirit, embodied in its female medium during possession.

sources.reference: Shona mhondoro ethnography

sacredAnimals.name: golden sunbirds
sacredAnimals.notes: Two beautiful golden sunbirds with which she brings out the sun.

sources.reference: Korekore oral tradition of Dzivaguru

attributes.name: skin patterned with all designs (kené)
attributes.notes: The cosmic anaconda's body bears every geometric design; these are the source of Shipibo kené art and the 'cosmic grid' linking the rivers to the Milky Way.

sources.reference: A. Gebhart-Sayer, The Cosmos Encoiled (1984); B. Illius on kené

sacredAnimals.name: anaconda / boa (ronin, rono)
sacredAnimals.notes: Ronin is itself the great water-serpent, ruler of the waters and mother of all waters.

sources.reference: Shipibo-Conibo cosmology; Gebhart-Sayer

attributes.name: the ripening heat of the sun
attributes.notes: 'Father Sun' (Bari), paired with Mother Moon, dwells in the topmost luminous world Jakon Nete and ripens the world with his heat.

sources.reference: P. G. Roe, The Cosmic Zygote (1982); Shipibo cosmology

attributes.name: rhythm-pounder figure (deble)
attributes.notes: Carved standing figures struck rhythmically on the ground in Poro funerary and initiation dances; male-female pairs represent the primordial couple Pombibele, 'those who gave birth'.

sources.reference: A. Glaze, Art and Death in a Senufo Village (1981)

sacredAnimals.name: hornbill (sejen / porpianong)
sacredAnimals.notes: The yellow-casqued hornbill, master among birds, is a symbol of fertility and the primordial-ancestor cult and a mythological founder of the Senufo; its long beak meeting a swollen belly figures dual male-female procreation.

sources.reference: Senufo art studies; Metropolitan Museum, Senufo hornbill (sejen)

attributes.name: cast-brass diviner's figures and amulets (yawiige)
attributes.notes: Sandobele diviners display brass and wooden spirit-figures and prescribe lost-wax brass charms made in the madebele's likeness for protection and healing.

sources.reference: A. Glaze, Art and Death in a Senufo Village (1981); Fowler Museum, Madebele divination couple

sacredAnimals.name: python (fo)
sacredAnimals.notes: The python (fo) is revered as the primary messenger between human communities and the madebele of the bush.

sources.reference: Senufo cosmology of the Fo python; Sandobele studies

sacredPlants.name: baobab
sacredPlants.notes: Offerings to Roog are made at the foot of sacred trees, pre-eminently the baobab.

sources.reference: H. Gravrand, La Civilisation Sereer

attributes.name: upright stone / tumulus abode
attributes.notes: Senegambian standing stones and earthen tumuli mark and house the pangool and serve as the loci of offering and invocation.

sources.reference: Studies of the Senegambian megaliths and Serer megalithic cult

sacredAnimals.name: serpent (often two coiled snakes)
sacredAnimals.notes: The pangool (sing. fangool, 'serpent') are symbolized by snakes, frequently depicted as two coiled serpents signifying vigilance and continuity.

sources.reference: Serer religion studies; Gravrand

sacredAnimals.name: crocodile
sacredAnimals.notes: Nyikang inherits a half-crocodile nature from his maternal line (the crocodile-goddess Nyakaya); crocodiles are protected in his connection.

sources.reference: W. Hofmayr, Die Schilluk (1925); E. E. Evans-Pritchard, The Divine Kingship of the Shilluk (1948)

sacredPlants.name: ambatch wood
sacredPlants.notes: Nyikang's and Dak's cult-effigies at the Akurwa shrine are made of light ambatch wood; the same wood furnished the effigy by which Dak (or Nyikang) cheated death.

sources.reference: E. E. Evans-Pritchard, The Divine Kingship of the Shilluk (1948)

sacredAnimals.name: crocodile
sacredAnimals.notes: Nyakaya is herself the crocodile-divinity of the Nile; she shifts between woman and crocodile and the crocodile is sacred to her line.

sources.reference: W. Hofmayr, Die Schilluk (1925); D. S. Oyler, Sudan Notes and Records

attributes.name: ambatch-wood effigy of himself
attributes.notes: A light-wood effigy substituted for Dak so that, when the whole community came to spear him, they killed the figure and his blood-vengeance was averted; the ambatch effigy of Dak stands beside Nyikang's at the Akurwa shrine.

sources.reference: E. E. Evans-Pritchard, The Divine Kingship of the Shilluk (1948); W. Hofmayr, Die Schilluk (1925)

attributes.name: Shabaka Stone
attributes.notes: A conglomerate stela (c. 710 BCE) on which Shabaka had the Memphite Theology re-engraved, presenting Ptah as creator of the world through heart (thought) and tongue (speech); later reused as a millstone.

sources.reference: Shabaka Stone, British Museum EA498

attributes.name: double uraeus
attributes.notes: Kushite kings of the 25th Dynasty, Shabaka among them, are distinctively shown with two rearing cobras (double uraeus) on the brow, asserting kingship over both Kush and Egypt.

sources.reference: Royal statuary of the 25th (Kushite) Dynasty
